ssc.label: No SSC
ssc.definition: Dead start or paused. No elastic contribution; force comes from rate of development alone.

ssc.label: Slow SSC
ssc.definition: Contact > 250 ms, large joint displacement. Countermovement assists the jump.

ssc.label: Fast SSC
ssc.definition: Contact < 250 ms, small displacement. Trains tendon stiffness and reactive strength.

ssc.label: Eccentric only
ssc.definition: Deceleration and landing. No concentric phase to train.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

exercises.name: Plank
exercises.position: The job is refusing lumbar extension while gravity pulls the pelvis down, so the demand is isometric and the spine stays neutral. Zero flexion load, which is why it survives on almost any lower-back programme.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, isometric. Time under tension is the dose.
cues: Ribs down, pelvis tucked slightly
Squeeze the glutes — it is a full-body brace
Stop when the hips start to sag, not at a time target

exercises.name: Dead Bug
exercises.position: Supine, so the spine is supported and the lower back can be pressed flat against the floor — the easiest place to learn a brace honestly, because any loss of position is immediately obvious as the back arching off the ground. The limbs provide the load, not weight.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, limb lever. Hardest with the limbs fully extended.
cues: Press the lower back into the floor and keep it there
Extend only as far as you hold position
Breathe out as the limbs reach

exercises.name: Hollow Hold
exercises.position: A plank turned over: the abdominals hold a slightly flexed spine against the lever of extended limbs. More demanding than a plank and more likely to be cheated by arching, which turns it into a hip-flexor hold.
cues: Lower back pressed down — no gap
Tuck the knees to regress
Stop the moment the back arches

exercises.name: Hollow Rock
exercises.position: A hollow hold with momentum added, so the trunk must keep its shape while the body rocks. The shape is the exercise — if the hollow breaks, the rocking is just thrashing.
cues: Rock from the shoulders, not the hips
Hold the hollow shape rigid
Regress to a static hold if the shape goes

exercises.name: Ab Rollout
exercises.position: The hardest anti-extension exercise here, because the lever lengthens as you roll out and the abdominals resist extension through range rather than isometrically. Still no deliberate lumbar flexion, so the cost is strength, not spinal load.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, lever-scaled by how far you roll.
cues: Ribs down the whole way out
Only roll as far as the back stays flat
From the knees first — feet is a long way up

exercises.name: Plank March
exercises.position: Lifting one point of contact makes the plank a rotational problem rather than purely an anti-extension one — the pelvis wants to twist and dip, and refusing that is the training effect.
cues: Hips stay square and level
Widen the feet to make it easier
Slow — speed hides the twist

exercises.name: Plank Pull Through
exercises.position: Reaching under the body to drag a weight adds an external rotational torque to the plank, so the load is adjustable in a way plank variations usually are not.
exercises.resistance: External, dragged. Scaled by the weight.
cues: Hips level — do not let them rotate toward the reaching arm
Drag, do not throw
Reset the plank between reps

exercises.name: Side Plank
exercises.position: The frontal-plane counterpart to the plank, and the only common exercise that loads the quadratus lumborum and lateral obliques isometrically without a bending moment on a loaded spine. Gluteus medius works hard on the down side.
cues: Stack the shoulders and hips in one line
Push the down hip up, do not let it sink
Knees down to regress

exercises.name: Star Side Plank
exercises.position: Lifting the top leg removes a point of support and loads both glute medius muscles at once — the bottom one isometrically, the top one concentrically. The hardest side plank variant without adding weight.
cues: Build a straight side plank first
Lift the leg without rolling backward
Stop when the hip drops

exercises.name: Side Plank Leg Lift
exercises.position: Holds the side plank while the top leg works dynamically, so trunk endurance and hip abduction strength are trained in the same set. For runners the glute medius demand is the point.
cues: Trunk stays rigid — only the leg moves
Lift to hip height, no higher
Toes forward, not turned up

exercises.name: QL Side Bend
exercises.position: Moves the spine into lateral flexion deliberately rather than resisting it — the opposite intent to a side plank despite working the same muscles. Lateral bending under load is a real spinal stressor, so it is a progression, not a starting point.
cues: Bend sideways only, no twisting
Small range to start
Stop at any pinching in the back

exercises.name: Side Bend
exercises.position: Adds external load to lateral flexion. Effective for the lateral trunk and one of the less forgiving things you can do to a lumbar spine, because the bending moment is both loaded and asymmetric.
cues: Pure sideways movement
No rotation, no forward lean
Light — this is not a loading exercise

exercises.name: Pallof Press
exercises.position: The reference anti-rotation exercise: a cable pulls the trunk into rotation and the job is to refuse it, with the torque increasing as the arms press further from the body. Loadable and spine-neutral, which is a rare combination in trunk work.
exercises.resistance: Cable or band. Torque peaks at full arm extension.
cues: Ribs down, hips square to the front
Press straight out from the sternum
Resist the twist rather than fighting it

exercises.name: Pallof Press In Split
exercises.position: A narrower, staggered base makes the pelvis harder to keep square, so the hip stabilizers join the anti-rotation demand. A step closer to how rotation is resisted in running and on the bike than a square stance is.
cues: Front foot forward, hips still square
Do not let the back hip open
Slower than the standing version

exercises.name: Anti-Rotation Landmine
exercises.position: The bar arcs overhead, so the rotational torque changes direction and magnitude continuously through the rep rather than staying constant like a cable. Heavier loading available than a Pallof press.
exercises.resistance: External, arcing. Torque varies through the range.
cues: Arms long, move the bar in an arc
Hips face forward throughout
Fight the bar, do not swing it

exercises.name: Half Kneeling Cross Chop
joints: shoulder flexion and adduction across the body
exercises.position: Rotation produced rather than resisted, with the half-kneeling base removing the legs' contribution so the rotation has to come from the trunk. The complement to a Pallof press — one builds the brake, the other the engine.
cues: Rotate through the ribs, not the lower back
Hips stay still in the half-kneeling position
Control the return

exercises.name: Cross Chop
exercises.position: Standing lets the hips drive the rotation, which is how rotation actually works in sport — the trunk transmits rather than originates it. Faster and more athletic than the half-kneeling version, and less isolating.
cues: Pivot the back foot and let the hip turn
Arms long, chop across and down
Finish balanced, not falling

exercises.name: Russian Twist
exercises.position: Seated rotation under load with the lumbar spine already flexed, which combines two of the stressors a sensitive back least enjoys — rotation and flexion together. Effective for the obliques and worth withholding from anyone with a flexion-intolerant back.
exercises.resistance: External, held. Hardest at the end of each rotation.
cues: Chest up — do not collapse into a slump
Rotate the ribs, not just the arms
Feet down to regress

exercises.name: Hanging Leg Raise
exercises.position: The first two-thirds is hip flexion and only the last part is genuine lumbar flexion, so most people train their hip flexors and call it abs. The spine is unloaded in compression because you are hanging, which makes it kinder than a sit-up despite the flexion.
cues: Curl the pelvis at the top — that is the abdominal part
No swinging
Bend the knees to regress

exercises.name: Reverse Crunch
exercises.position: Moves the pelvis toward the ribs rather than the ribs toward the pelvis, which is the half of trunk flexion a sit-up neglects. Supine and unloaded, so the flexion cost is low.
cues: Curl the tailbone up off the floor
Slow — do not use momentum from the legs
Keep the lower back in contact until the curl

exercises.name: V-Up
exercises.position: Both ends of the body lift at once, so the abdominals shorten through full range against a long double lever. Repeated full lumbar flexion, which is the training stimulus and the contraindication in the same sentence.
cues: Reach hands to feet, not past them
Lower under control
Tuck the knees to regress

exercises.name: Single Leg V-Up
exercises.position: One leg halves the lever and adds a small anti-rotation demand, which makes it both a regression of the V-up and a slightly different exercise.
cues: Keep the hips square
Non-working leg stays down and still
Alternate sides evenly

exercises.name: Sit-Up
exercises.position: Past the first third the hip flexors do most of the work, pulling on the lumbar spine from the front of the vertebrae. Repeated loaded flexion plus hip-flexor traction is the combination most commonly implicated in low-back aggravation from ab training.
cues: Curl up rather than hinging at the hips
Do not anchor the feet if you can avoid it
Choose a plank instead if the back complains

exercises.name: GHD Sit-up
joints: lumbar extension then full flexion (maximal range)
exercises.position: Takes the lumbar spine from hyperextension to full flexion under bodyweight at speed — the largest loaded spinal range in the bank, and the exercise most likely to injure someone who is not prepared for it. Powerful when earned, reckless when prescribed early.
cues: Start with a very small range and build over weeks
Hands touch the floor only when the range is earned
Never prescribe this to an unprepared back

exercises.name: Dragon Flag
exercises.position: The longest possible lever against trunk extension — the whole body lowered as one rigid unit from the shoulders. Spine stays neutral throughout, so the difficulty is pure strength rather than range, but the demand is extreme.
cues: One rigid line — no hinging at the hips
Bend the knees to shorten the lever
Lower only as far as you keep the line

exercises.name: Windshield Wiper
exercises.position: Rotating a long loaded lever, which puts significant torsional stress on the lumbar discs at end range. Strong oblique stimulus with the highest rotational cost in the block.
cues: Shoulders stay flat on the floor
Control the whole arc
Bend the knees to regress

exercises.name: Back Extension
exercises.position: Trains the spinal extensors concentrically through range, which almost nothing else in this bank does — planks hold them isometrically and hinges load them isometrically. The bottom of the range involves flexion, so range should be earned.
cues: Finish level, do not hyperextend past neutral
Lead with the glutes
Small range first

exercises.name: Back Extension Hold
exercises.position: Holding neutral rather than moving through range, so the extensors work isometrically with no flexion at the bottom. The version to use when endurance is the goal and spinal range is a concern — which for endurance athletes holding a position for hours is usually the case.
cues: Hold level — ears, shoulders and hips in line
Breathe normally through the hold
Stop when position goes, not when the clock does

exercises.name: Reverse Hyper
exercises.position: Torso fixed and the legs move, so the hip extensors work while the spine is lightly traction-loaded rather than compressed. Widely used for lumbar-tolerant posterior chain work for exactly that reason.
cues: Drive with the glutes, not a swing
Stop at level
Control the return — no pendulum

exercises.name: Superman Hold
exercises.position: The zero-equipment spinal extensor hold. Prone on the floor, so there is no apparatus and no load beyond limb weight — the entry point for posterior-chain endurance when a bench or GHD is not available.
cues: Lift just enough to clear the floor
Lengthen rather than crunching backward
Look down, not up

exercises.name: Jefferson Curl
exercises.position: Deliberately loads spinal flexion segment by segment, the exact thing every other entry here is coached to avoid. Used to build tissue tolerance to flexion under very light load; prescribed carelessly it is the single riskiest exercise in the bank.
exercises.resistance: External, very light. Hardest at full flexion.
cues: Start with no weight at all
Roll down one vertebra at a time
Not for an acutely painful or flexion-intolerant back

flags.text: Loaded end-range spinal flexion is contested. Some coaches use Jefferson curls to build flexion tolerance; others consider the risk unjustifiable. The bank carries it because it exists and is widely prescribed, not as a recommendation — this is one of the entries most in need of a qualified sign-off before any athlete sees it.

exercises.name: Death March
exercises.position: A single-leg RDL repeated as a walk, so the hamstrings work at length under continuous tension while the trunk resists both flexion and rotation each step. Loads hang from the hands, so the spine is in traction rather than compression.
cues: Reach the back heel to the wall behind you
Hips square each step
Slow — this is not a walk with weights

swap_edges.same: Anterior trunk work, bodyweight, no equipment
swap_edges.changed: Isometric anti-extension instead of repeated loaded lumbar flexion
Spine stays flat on the floor — no flexion at all
Removes the largest loaded spinal range in the bank

swap_edges.same: Hard anterior trunk work with a long lever
swap_edges.changed: Resists extension instead of producing full flexion

swap_edges.same: Anterior trunk, long double lever, bodyweight
swap_edges.changed: Isometric hold rather than repeated full flexion
Anti-rotation with a neutral spine instead of loaded rotation in flexion
No end-range lumbar torsion under a long lever
Resists side bend while walking rather than producing it under load
Isometric, no loaded bending moment
Holds neutral instead of loading full flexion
Isometric at neutral, so no flexion at the bottom of the range

swap_edges.same: Posterior chain and spinal extensor work
swap_edges.changed: Torso fixed and legs move, so the spine is tractioned rather than flexed
Isometric rather than moving into lateral flexion
No wheel or barbell; isometric rather than through range
Bodyweight — the limb lift supplies the rotational torque
Cable or band instead of a barbell and landmine
No bar needed; supine instead of hanging
Floor instead of a bench or GHD; isometric
No apparatus at all
Floor instead of a GHD, and a far smaller range
No loaded shoulder flexion at a long lever
Much smaller range, no hyperextended start
Static hold on the floor instead of an eccentric lower
Isometric, with no lengthening lever
Both feet down, so a wider base and less abduction demand
Limbs move one at a time with the back supported

swap_edges.same: Trunk flexion with a long lever
swap_edges.changed: One leg halves the lever
On the spot instead of walking 20 m
